Photosensitisation requires oxygen, sunlight, photodynamic chemicals, and skin devoid of hair/wool/pigment — unprotected skin is necessary for UV light to reach and activate the photodynamic chemicals.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Fully pigmented, haired skin: This would actually protect against photosensitisation by blocking UV penetration — the opposite of a requirement.
  • C. Cold ambient temperature: Not a listed requirement; sunlight/UV exposure is the key environmental factor, not temperature.
  • D. Absence of oxygen: Incorrect — oxygen (for reactive oxygen species generation) is actually required, not its absence.

posts.post_content: Enlargement of the remaining kidney after unilateral nephrectomy is an example of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Compensatory renal hypertrophy after unilateral nephrectomy is a form of hypertrophy, where cell size (not cell number) increases in the remaining kidney.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Pathological hyperplasia: Involves an increase in cell number under excess hormone/growth factor stimulation (e.g. cystic endometrial hyperplasia), not the cell-size-only change of compensatory renal hypertrophy.
  • C. Metaplasia: A change of one adult cell type to another, unrelated to compensatory organ enlargement.
  • D. Dysplasia: A disordered pattern of tissue maturation, unrelated to physiological compensatory enlargement.

posts.post_content: The gelatinous, translucent appearance of adipose tissue seen in severe atrophy is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Serous atrophy of fat describes the gelatinous appearance of adipose tissue in severely atrophied/emaciated animals, one of the gross features of atrophy alongside decreased weight/volume and a wrinkled surface.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Fatty change: Refers to abnormal lipid accumulation within cells (e.g. hepatic lipidosis), the opposite process from fat loss/atrophy.
  • C. Lipomatosis: Refers to excess/overgrowth of fatty tissue, not its atrophic, gelatinous depletion.
  • D. Ceroid deposition: Refers to an early/pathological form of lipofuscin pigment accumulation, not the gelatinous change of fat atrophy.

posts.post_content: Chemotaxis is best defined as:

_aimcq_options.text: Unidirectional migration of cells toward a chemical attractant
RBC movement outside vessels during inflammation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Chemotaxis is unidirectional migration of leucocytes toward a chemical attractant, which may be exogenous (bacterial products) or endogenous (C5a, Leukotriene B4, cytokines).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Random, non-directional cell movement: This is the opposite of chemotaxis, which is specifically directed movement.
  • C. Adhesion of leucocytes to endothelium: Describes the adhesion step (mediated by integrins/ICAM) in leucocyte emigration, a step preceding chemotaxis, not chemotaxis itself.
  • D. RBC movement outside vessels during inflammation: This describes diapedesis, a distinct process from chemotaxis (which involves directed leucocyte migration).

posts.post_content: Rabbits with tuberculosis rarely form suppurative lesions because:

_aimcq_options.text: An antienzyme inhibits proteases needed for pus formation
TB in rabbits causes only serous inflammation
Rabbits are naturally resistant to TB infection

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rabbits with TB rarely suppurate because an antienzyme against proteases inhibits the proteolysis required for pus formation, even though necrosis and neutrophils may be present.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. They lack neutrophils entirely: Incorrect — rabbits are not devoid of neutrophils; the block is at the level of proteolytic enzyme activity, not neutrophil availability.
  • C. TB in rabbits causes only serous inflammation: Not accurate — TB classically causes granulomatous/caseating inflammation, not simply serous inflammation.
  • D. Rabbits are naturally resistant to TB infection: Incorrect — rabbits can be infected by TB; the point relates specifically to their reduced capacity to suppurate, not to resistance against infection itself.

posts.post_content: "Bread-and-butter" appearance of the pericardium is characteristic of which type of inflammation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The classic "bread-and-butter" appearance of the pericardium describes fibrinous pericarditis, in which a stringy, yellow fibrin net covers the epicardial/pericardial surfaces.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Serous: Produces a thin, plasma-like effusion, not the stringy fibrin appearance described.
  • C. Suppurative: Produces pus (necrosis + neutrophils + proteolysis), a different gross appearance from the fibrinous "bread-and-butter" pattern.
  • D. Catarrhal: Involves mucus from mucus-producing epithelium, which is not relevant to the pericardium (a serous membrane, not a mucus-secreting one).

posts.post_content: Which arachidonic acid metabolite, generated via the cyclooxygenase pathway, causes vasoconstriction (opposite to PGI2/PGE2/PGD2)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Thromboxane A2, produced via the cyclooxygenase pathway, causes vasoconstriction, in contrast to PGI2, PGE2, and PGD2, which cause vasodilation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Leukotriene B4: A product of the 5-lipoxygenase (not cyclooxygenase) pathway, and functions mainly as a chemotactic agent rather than a vasoconstrictor.
  • C. Prostaglandin E2: A cyclooxygenase product, but causes vasodilation, the opposite effect from thromboxane A2.
  • D. Nitric oxide: Causes vasodilation and is not a cyclooxygenase pathway product.

posts.post_content: Which chemokine class (α, C-X-C) primarily attracts neutrophils?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

α (C-X-C) chemokines primarily attract neutrophils.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. β (C-C) chemokines: Attract monocytes, lymphocytes, eosinophils, and basophils, not primarily neutrophils.
  • C. γ (C) chemokines: Attract lymphocytes specifically, not neutrophils.
  • D. CX3C chemokines: Attract monocytes and T-cells, not primarily neutrophils.

posts.post_content: Haptoglobin, an acute phase protein synthesised by the liver, functions primarily to:

_aimcq_options.text: Bind haemoglobin and act as an antioxidant
Form the backbone of the complement system

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Haptoglobin, an IL-1/TNF-driven acute phase protein, binds free haemoglobin and acts as an antioxidant.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Form the backbone of the complement system: This is the role of C3, not haptoglobin.
  • C. Opsonise bacteria for phagocytosis: This is primarily the role of C-reactive protein (CRP) among the acute phase proteins, not haptoglobin.
  • D. Provide antiviral defence: This is the role of interferons, not haptoglobin.

posts.post_content: The granules of basophils and mast cells characteristically contain:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Basophil/mast cell granules contain heparin and histamine (plus proteolytic enzymes in mast cells), released via IgE-triggered degranulation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Myeloperoxidase and hypochlorous radical: These are part of the neutrophil killing mechanism (H₂O₂ + myeloperoxidase → hypochlorous radical), not basophil/mast cell granule content.
  • C. Perforin and granzyme: Associated with cytotoxic T lymphocyte/NK cell killing mechanisms, not basophil/mast cell granules.
  • D. Lysozyme only: Lysozyme is a neutrophil-associated enzyme hydrolysing bacterial peptidoglycan, not the primary basophil/mast cell granule content.

posts.post_content: The eccentric "cart-wheel" nucleus is a classic morphological feature of which inflammatory cell?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The plasma cell, arising from B lymphocytes and responsible for antibody production, classically shows an eccentric "cart-wheel" nucleus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Lymphocyte: Has a round nucleus occupying most of the cell, not the eccentric cart-wheel pattern of a plasma cell.
  • C. Macrophage: Has a nucleus with 1–2 nucleoli, distinct from the plasma cell's cart-wheel appearance.
  • D. Eosinophil: Has a bilobed nucleus, not the eccentric cart-wheel pattern.

posts.post_title: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura vs Fever Signs
posts.post_content: Which of the following is listed among the clinical signs of fever?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Clinical signs of fever include anorexia, somnolence, malaise, and shivering/chills, reflecting the systemic metabolic, endocrine and autonomic effects of pyrogen-driven hypothalamic thermostat resetting.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Polyuria: Not a listed clinical sign of fever in this framework.
  • C. Hyperphagia (increased appetite): The opposite occurs — fever is associated with anorexia (decreased appetite), not increased appetite.
  • D. Hypothermia: The opposite of fever's core feature, which is increased body temperature, not decreased.

posts.post_content: Which cyclin-CDK complex regulates the M (mitosis) phase of the cell cycle?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Cyclin B/CDK1 regulates the M (mitosis) phase of the cell cycle.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cyclin D/CDK4: Regulates the G1 phase, not mitosis.
  • B. Cyclin A/CDK1: Regulates the S phase (DNA synthesis), not mitosis.
  • D. Cyclin D/CDK2: Also regulates the G1 phase, not the M phase.

posts.post_content: Basic Fibroblast Growth Factor (bFGF), important in angiogenesis and wound repair, is primarily produced by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Basic FGF is primarily produced by macrophages, while acidic FGF derives from neural tissue; both promote angiogenesis, cell migration, wound repair, and haematopoiesis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Neural tissue: This is the source of acidic FGF, not the basic form specifically asked about.
  • C. Platelets: The primary source of PDGF and TGF-β, not the primary source described for basic FGF.
  • D. T lymphocytes: A source of TGF-β, not the primary source of basic FGF.

posts.post_content: Which of the following is classified as a local (as opposed to systemic) factor that delays wound healing?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The presence of a foreign body is a local factor delaying wound healing, along with infection, mechanical movement, wound size/location/type, and cold.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Diabetes mellitus: A systemic factor affecting wound healing throughout the body, not a local factor.
  • B. Vitamin C deficiency: A systemic nutritional factor impairing collagen synthesis, not local.
  • D. Hyperadrenocorticism: A systemic endocrine factor impairing healing, not a local factor.

posts.post_content: Idiopathic polyneuritis ("Coonhound paralysis") typically develops following:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Idiopathic polyneuritis (Coonhound paralysis) typically develops 7–14 days after a raccoon scratch or bite, producing ascending symmetric paralysis with segmental demyelination.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Influenza infection: This is the trigger for cauda equina neuritis (a Guillain-Barré-like condition in horses), not Coonhound paralysis.
  • C. Vaccination: Not the classic trigger described for Coonhound paralysis.
  • D. Tick bite: Not the classic trigger; the condition is specifically linked to raccoon exposure.

posts.post_content: Cold haemagglutinin disease, seen in dogs and horses, is mediated by which antibody class and produces lesions primarily where?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Cold haemagglutinin disease is mediated by cold-triggered IgM autoantibodies, producing capillary stasis and agglutination with lesions of the nose, ears, and extremities.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. IgG antibodies; affecting the liver: Neither the correct antibody class nor the correct target site for this disease.
  • C. IgA antibodies; affecting the gut: Not the antibody class or affected site for cold haemagglutinin disease.
  • D. IgE antibodies; affecting the lungs: IgE is associated with Type I hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis, not cold haemagglutinin disease, and the lungs are not the classic target site here.

posts.post_content: Renal amyloidosis typically produces which gross appearance of the kidney?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Renal amyloidosis typically produces a swollen, pale, mottled, yellow-orange kidney, which can progress to glomerular filtration failure, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, and uraemia.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Small, contracted, scarred: More typical of chronic interstitial nephritis/end-stage kidney disease, not the classic amyloid appearance.
  • C. Cystic, honeycombed: Suggestive of polycystic kidney disease, not amyloidosis.
  • D. Normal size with black discolouration: Not the characteristic gross appearance of renal amyloid deposition.

posts.post_content: A malignant tumour of adipose tissue is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A malignant tumour of adipose tissue is termed liposarcoma, following the mesenchymal malignant suffix "-sarcoma".

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Lipoma: This is the benign counterpart tumour of adipose tissue, not the malignant form.
  • C. Adipocarcinoma: Not correct nomenclature — since adipose tissue is mesenchymal in origin, its malignant tumour takes the "-sarcoma" suffix, not "-carcinoma" (reserved for epithelial malignancies).
  • D. Chondrosarcoma: This is the malignant tumour of cartilage, not adipose tissue.

posts.post_content: The C3H strain of mice is classically used to study the hereditary predisposition to which tumour type?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The C3H mouse strain is classically used to demonstrate hereditary predisposition to mammary and liver tumours.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Osteosarcoma: Not the tumour type classically associated with the C3H mouse strain in this hereditary predisposition context.
  • C. Renal cell carcinoma: Not associated with the C3H strain example given.
  • D. Melanoma: The classic hereditary predisposition example for melanoma in domestic animals is grey/white horses, not the C3H mouse strain.

posts.post_content: Indirect-acting chemical carcinogens (procarcinogens), such as polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosoamines, require:

_aimcq_options.text: No activation — they act directly on DNA

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Indirect-acting carcinogens (procarcinogens), such as polycyclic hydrocarbons (e.g. benzanthracene) and nitrosoamines (e.g. vinyl chloride, aldrin, dieldrin), require metabolic activation before they become carcinogenic.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. No activation — they act directly on DNA: This describes direct-acting agents (e.g. alkylating agents like β-propiolactone), the opposite category from indirect-acting procarcinogens.
  • C. UV light exposure only: UV/solar radiation is a separate physical carcinogenesis mechanism (pyrimidine dimers), not the activation route for these chemical procarcinogens.
  • D. Co-administration with vitamin supplements: Not a recognised activation mechanism for procarcinogens.

posts.post_content: Metastatic homing of lung cancer classically favours which organ, while typically sparing skeletal muscle?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Lung cancer classically shows metastatic homing to the adrenal gland, while typically sparing skeletal muscle — homing depends on primary tumour location, vascular/lymphatic drainage, and organ tropism.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Spleen: Not the classic homing site cited for lung cancer metastasis in this context.
  • C. Pancreas: Not the organ specifically identified as the classic homing site for lung cancer.
  • D. Thyroid: Not the organ described as the classic metastatic homing site for lung cancer.

posts.post_content: Ectopic ACTH secretion by a lung tumour, unrelated to the tumour's native tissue type, exemplifies:

_aimcq_options.text: Direct hormonal effect of the native tissue

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Ectopic hormone production not native to the tumour's tissue of origin — such as a lung tumour secreting ACTH, or fibrosarcoma secreting insulin — exemplifies paraneoplastic syndrome.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Direct hormonal effect of the native tissue: This would describe a hormone-secreting tumour arising from an endocrine tissue itself (e.g. insulinoma → hypoglycaemia), not ectopic production by unrelated tissue.
  • C. Cancer cachexia: A TNF-α driven wasting syndrome, a distinct phenomenon from ectopic hormone secretion.
  • D. Pressure atrophy: A mechanical effect of tumour growth on adjacent tissue, unrelated to ectopic hormone secretion.
